analysis.title: Global Rates Notes: 4Q26 Treasury Refunding Preview
key_insights: GS expects Treasury to lower its near-term borrowing projections at its financing estimate release at 3pm on Monday, November 2, partly because of a higher starting cash balance. GS estimates marketable borrowing of $571bn for 4Q26, including $286bn of net bills.

The rise in yields and the increase in buyback operations have put focus on long-end supply. GS sees a risk that Treasury cuts long-end auction sizes after the August change in guidance and the mid-August increase in long-end buybacks, but this is not its base case.
GS base case: Treasury maintains or modestly increases buyback envelope sizes, keeps 10-to-30y auction sizes steady, and begins increasing 2-to-7y auction sizes in May 2027.
GS rules out eliminating the 20y point only with difficulty. Treasury's surprise buyback increase was a clear departure from prior behavior, so a more dramatic step cannot be strictly excluded.

Four reasons for steady 10-to-30y sizes: fiscal needs reinforce the value of liquid benchmark points, limited room to cut 20y sizes before liquidity suffers, prior guidance of unchanged sizes for at least the next several quarters, and little sign of market indigestion from long-end supply.

GS sees buybacks as a more flexible tool for managing the maturity composition of debt. Describing them explicitly as a maturity-management tool, instead of only liquidity support, could raise their market impact if Treasury becomes less price sensitive in operations.

GS expects Treasury to change its guidance to nod toward future auction size adjustments, with two-sided wording ('changes' rather than 'increases'). One possible rewrite: 'Treasury anticipates it may be appropriate to consider changes to nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes over the next several quarters.'

GS argues larger long-end buybacks have compressed long-end dispersion and helped spreads (Exhibit 2). Buying back off-the-run issues while keeping on-the-run sizes adequate should support liquidity and supply absorption.

Demand trends: less price-sensitive non-Fed investors have a smaller footprint, foreign official buyers are unlikely to add net demand without material dollar weakness, and defined benefit pension demand for the long end is shrinking on both sides of the Atlantic.

Because foreign demand is mostly private and domestic demand relies on money funds, asset managers, banks and hedge funds, GS sees a case for more front-end and belly supply. Treasury can keep relying meaningfully on T-bills.

GS expects the Fed to keep adding Treasuries through bill purchases until it reaches a market-consistent share, which it estimates happens in 2028. It expects this demand to be somewhat vol dampening.

GS estimates 1Q27 marketable borrowing of $713bn, assuming a $900bn end-of-quarter cash balance target. Its deficit projections are $2.0tn/$2.1tn/$2.1tn for FY27/28/29, modestly below its prior baseline because of larger than expected corporate tax receipts.

risk_factors: Treasury could cut long-end auction sizes, which is not GS's base case.
Treasury could take a more dramatic step such as eliminating the 20y point, given its surprise buyback increase.
A guidance change that flags auction size adjustments could move long-end pricing.
Foreign official demand is unlikely to rise without material dollar weakness, and long-end pension demand is dwindling.
charts_described: Exhibit 2 plots the change in SOFR swap spreads since August 18th against starting spread levels. The text says widening has been most pronounced at points that started tighter.
Exhibit 5 gives projected monthly coupon auction sizes, with unchanged sizes through 1Q27 and gradual increases limited to 2-to-7y maturities afterward.
vol_and_positioning: GS expects Fed bill purchases to be somewhat vol dampening, as the pace depends on funding conditions.

GS says leaning on front-end and intermediate coupon supply could reduce interest expense volatility, and proactive supply mix management reduces the risk of supply imbalances worsening rate volatility at particular curve points.
Long-end swap spread widening since the August 18 buyback upsizing announcement has been most pronounced at points that started tighter (Exhibit 2).

tension_points.bull_case: GS base case is that Treasury keeps 10-to-30y auction sizes steady, citing fiscal needs, limited room to cut the 20y, prior guidance of unchanged sizes, and no sign of long-end indigestion.
tension_points.bear_case: Treasury could cut long-end auction sizes, or even eliminate the 20y point, after the August guidance tweak to 'changes' and the surprise buyback increase.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Refunding guidance that replaces 'maintaining nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes for at least the next several quarters' with language on considering changes to auction sizes, or an announced cut to 10-to-30y sizes.

theme_stances.evidence: keep 10-to-30y auction sizes steady, and eventually begin to increase 2-to-7y auction sizes

theme_stances.key_argument: Buybacks are a more flexible tool for managing the maturity composition of debt than auction sizes.
theme_stances.evidence: buybacks offer a more flexible tool for managing the maturity composition of debt outstanding
